assessment.name: Year 8 Autumn 2 Diagnostic Assessment
assessment.sections: Section A: 45 multiple choice questions. Section B: written response.
assessment.weighting: 60% Year 8 units (B2.1, C2.1, P2.1). 40% Year 7 units.
assessment.equipment: Chromebook, 2 black or blue pens, pencil, ruler, rubber, calculator

leitner_plan.new: C2.1 Acids and alkalis (5), P2.1 Movement and pressure (4)

leitner_plan.quiz: B1.2 quiz, then C1.2 and P1.2

leitner_plan.new: P1.3 Energy (4), P1.4 Circuits (3), 2 summary cards

leitner_plan.quiz: Retry your 2 weakest topics from the mock

cards.title: The skeleton and joints
cards.question: What are the four jobs of the skeleton, and how are bones held together at a joint?
points: Support: holds the body up and gives it shape.
Protection: the skull protects the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs.
Movement: muscles pull on bones. Making blood cells: in the bone marrow.
Joints are where bones meet: hinge (knee, elbow), ball and socket (hip, shoulder), fixed (skull).
Ligaments hold bone to bone. Cartilage covers the ends of bones so they do not rub.
cards.watch_out: Ligaments join bone to bone. Tendons join muscle to bone. Do not mix them up.

cards.title: Muscles and movement
cards.question: How do antagonistic muscles work together to bend and straighten your arm?
points: Muscles can only pull (contract). They cannot push.
Muscles work in antagonistic pairs. When one contracts, the other relaxes.
To bend the arm: biceps contracts, triceps relaxes.
To straighten the arm: triceps contracts, biceps relaxes.
Tendons attach muscles to bones, so a contracting muscle pulls the bone.
cards.watch_out: A relaxing muscle does not push the bone back. The other muscle in the pair pulls it.

cards.title: The breathing system and gas exchange
cards.question: What path does air take into the lungs, and how are the alveoli adapted for gas exchange?
points: Air path: nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Rings of cartilage keep the trachea open.
In the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood.
Alveoli are adapted: walls one cell thick, huge surface area, moist, rich blood supply (capillaries).

example.heading: Gases in and out
lines: Breathed in air: more oxygen, less carbon dioxide.
Breathed out air: less oxygen, more carbon dioxide, more water vapour.

cards.watch_out: Breathing is moving air in and out. Respiration is the reaction in cells that releases energy.

cards.title: Breathing in and out
cards.question: What happens to the diaphragm, ribs, volume and pressure when you breathe in?
points: Breathing in: diaphragm contracts and flattens; intercostal muscles contract, ribs move up and out.
Chest volume increases, so pressure inside falls and air rushes in.
Breathing out: diaphragm relaxes and moves up; ribs move down and in.
Chest volume decreases, so pressure rises and air is pushed out.
Bell jar model: balloons are the lungs, rubber sheet is the diaphragm. It has no ribs, which is a weakness.
cards.watch_out: Air always moves from high pressure to low pressure.

cards.title: Drugs
cards.question: What is a drug, and what is the difference between medicinal and recreational drugs?
points: A drug is a chemical that changes the way your body works.
Medicinal drugs help your health, such as paracetamol (painkiller) and antibiotics (kill bacteria).
Recreational drugs are taken for enjoyment, not health. Some are legal (caffeine, alcohol, nicotine); many are illegal (cannabis).
Addiction means the body depends on a drug. Stopping causes withdrawal symptoms.
cards.watch_out: Legal does not mean safe. Alcohol and nicotine are legal for adults but harm the body.

cards.title: Alcohol and smoking
cards.question: How do alcohol and smoking damage the body?
points: Alcohol is a depressant. It slows down the nervous system, so reactions are slower.
Long term, alcohol damages the liver and brain.
Tar in cigarette smoke causes cancer and damages the cilia that sweep mucus out of the lungs.
Nicotine is addictive. Carbon monoxide reduces how much oxygen the blood can carry.
Alcohol and nicotine can cross the placenta and harm an unborn baby.
cards.watch_out: Smoker's cough happens because damaged cilia cannot clear mucus, so the person coughs it up.

cards.title: Plant organs
cards.question: What are the main organs of a plant and what does each one do?
points: Roots: anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals. Root hair cells give a large surface area.
Stem: holds the plant up and carries substances between roots and leaves.
Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem carries sugars around the plant.
Leaf: the organ where photosynthesis happens.
Flower: the organ for sexual reproduction.
cards.watch_out: Root hair cells have no chloroplasts. They are underground, so there is no light for photosynthesis.

cards.title: Leaf structure
cards.question: How is a leaf built to do photosynthesis well?
points: Leaves are broad and flat for a large surface area to absorb light.
The palisade layer near the top is packed with chloroplasts.
The spongy layer has air spaces so gases can move through the leaf.
Stomata (tiny holes, mostly underneath) let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
Guard cells open and close the stomata. A waxy layer on top cuts water loss.

example.heading: Photosynthesis word equation
lines: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (needs light and chlorophyll)

cards.watch_out: Stomata are holes. Guard cells are the cells either side that open and close them.

cards.title: Acids, alkalis and the pH scale
cards.question: What does the pH scale tell you, and what are some common acids and alkalis?
points: pH runs from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acid, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkali.
The lower the pH, the more acidic. The higher the pH, the more alkaline.
Acids: hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric, citric (lemons), ethanoic (vinegar).
Alkalis: sodium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide. Found in soap and oven cleaner.
A base neutralises an acid. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
cards.watch_out: Concentrated means lots of acid particles in a small volume. Dilute means more water was added.

cards.title: Indicators
cards.question: What is an indicator, and what colours do litmus and universal indicator turn?
points: An indicator changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline.
Litmus: turns red in acid and blue in alkali. Purple in neutral.
Universal indicator shows the pH: red (strong acid), orange or yellow (weak acid), green (neutral, pH 7), blue (weak alkali), purple (strong alkali).
Red cabbage juice is a natural indicator.
A pH probe or meter gives a more precise number than an indicator.
cards.watch_out: Litmus only tells you acid or alkali. Universal indicator tells you how strong.

cards.title: Neutralisation
cards.question: What happens when an acid reacts with an alkali, and where is this used in everyday life?
points: acid + alkali → salt + water. This is neutralisation.
Adding alkali to acid makes the pH rise towards 7.
Indigestion tablets neutralise extra stomach acid.
Farmers add lime to acidic soil. Toothpaste neutralises acid in your mouth.

example.heading: Example word equation
lines: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water

cards.watch_out: Salt in chemistry means any compound made this way, not just table salt (sodium chloride).

cards.title: Naming salts and word equations
cards.question: How do you name the salt made in a reaction, and how do you write a word equation?
points: The first part of the salt name comes from the metal. The second part comes from the acid.
hydrochloric acid → chloride. sulfuric acid → sulfate. nitric acid → nitrate.
Reactants go on the left, products on the right. The arrow means reacts to make.
A plus sign means and. Never use an equals sign.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen
copper oxide + nitric acid → copper nitrate + water

cards.watch_out: Chloride ends in ide. Chlorine is the element; chloride is in the salt name.

cards.title: Acids with metals and carbonates
cards.question: What is made when an acid reacts with a metal or a carbonate, and how do you test for the gases?
points: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen
Test for hydrogen: a lit splint gives a squeaky pop.
carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide
Test for carbon dioxide: bubble it through limewater, which turns milky (cloudy).
Bubbling (fizzing) shows a gas is being made. Copper and gold do not react with dilute acids.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide

cards.watch_out: Squeaky pop is hydrogen. Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Limewater is for carbon dioxide.

cards.title: Speed
cards.question: How do you calculate speed, and what is relative motion?
points: speed = distance ÷ time
Units: metres per second (m/s), or kilometres per hour (km/h).
Average speed uses the total distance and total time of a journey.
Relative motion is how fast one object moves compared with another.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s.
speed = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s
Rearranged: distance = speed × time; time = distance ÷ speed

cards.watch_out: Check units first. Change km to m (× 1000) and minutes to seconds (× 60) if needed.

cards.title: Distance-time graphs
cards.question: How do you read speed and stopping from a distance-time graph?
points: Distance goes up the side, time goes along the bottom.
The steeper the line, the faster the object is moving.
A straight sloping line means a steady speed.
A flat (horizontal) line means the object has stopped.
A curved line means the speed is changing.

example.heading: Speed from the slope
lines: Line rises 60 m in 12 s.
speed = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 m/s

cards.watch_out: A flat line on a distance-time graph means stationary, not moving at a steady speed.

cards.title: Pressure on surfaces
cards.question: How do you calculate pressure, and why do snowshoes stop you sinking?
points: pressure = force ÷ area
Units: N/m² (also called pascals, Pa) or N/cm².
Bigger area means smaller pressure: snowshoes, tractor tyres, wide straps on a bag.
Smaller area means bigger pressure: a sharp knife, a drawing pin, football studs.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A 600 N person stands on 0.03 m² of shoe.
pressure = 600 ÷ 0.03 = 20 000 N/m²

cards.watch_out: Area in cm² gives N/cm². Area in m² gives N/m². Write the right unit.

cards.title: Pressure in liquids and gases
cards.question: How does pressure change with depth in water and with height in the air?
points: Liquid pressure increases with depth because there is more water pushing down from above.
Dams are thicker at the bottom. Water spurts furthest from the lowest hole in a bottle.
Gas pressure comes from particles hitting the walls of the container.
Atmospheric pressure falls as you go higher because there is less air above you.
Upthrust is the upward push from a liquid. An object floats when upthrust equals its weight.
cards.watch_out: Liquids cannot be squashed, so pushing on them passes the pressure on. This is how hydraulic brakes work.

cards.title: Animal and plant cells
cards.question: Which parts do animal and plant cells share, and which are only in plant cells?
points: Nucleus: controls the cell and holds genetic material.
Cell membrane: controls what goes in and out. Cytoplasm: where reactions happen.
Mitochondria: where respiration releases energy.
Plant cells also have: a cell wall (strengthens), chloroplasts (photosynthesis), a vacuole full of cell sap (keeps the cell firm).
cards.watch_out: Plant cells have a cell membrane AND a cell wall. They have mitochondria too.

cards.title: Specialised cells
cards.question: How are sperm, red blood, nerve and root hair cells adapted to their jobs?
points: Sperm cell: tail to swim, lots of mitochondria for energy.
Egg cell: food store in the cytoplasm.
Red blood cell: no nucleus, so more room to carry oxygen.
Nerve cell: long, to carry electrical signals around the body.
Root hair cell: long hair gives a big surface area to absorb water. Ciliated cells sweep mucus.
cards.watch_out: Unicellular organisms (amoeba, euglena) are one cell that does every job.

cards.title: Using a microscope
cards.question: How do you use a light microscope safely, and how do you work out magnification?
points: Parts include the eyepiece lens, objective lenses, stage, clips, light and focusing wheels.
Start with the lowest power objective lens.
Use the coarse focus first, then the fine focus.
Make a slide with a thin sample, add a stain (iodine for onion cells), lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.

example.heading: Total magnification
lines: eyepiece × objective

cards.watch_out: Watch from the side while moving the stage up, so the lens does not crash into the slide.

cards.title: Organisation and diffusion
cards.question: How are cells organised into a whole organism, and how do substances get into cells?
points: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Tissue: group of similar cells doing one job (muscle tissue).
Organ: different tissues working together (heart, stomach, leaf).
Organ system: organs working together (digestive system).
Diffusion moves substances such as oxygen and glucose into cells, from high concentration to low.
cards.watch_out: The heart is an organ, not a tissue. It is made from several tissues.

cards.title: States of matter and the particle model
cards.question: How are particles arranged and how do they move in solids, liquids and gases?
points: Solid: fixed shape and volume. Particles touching in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot.
Liquid: fixed volume, takes the shape of its container. Particles touching but random, slide past each other.
Gas: fills its container. Particles far apart, moving fast in all directions.
Gases can be squashed (compressed) because of the big gaps between particles.
cards.watch_out: Particles do not get bigger when heated. They move more and spread out.

cards.title: Changing state
cards.question: What are the names of the changes of state, and what happens to the particles?
points: Melting: solid → liquid. Freezing: liquid → solid.
Boiling and evaporating: liquid → gas. Condensing: gas → liquid.
Sublimation: solid → gas directly (dry ice).
Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
Evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature. Boiling happens all through the liquid at the boiling point.
cards.watch_out: Mass stays the same when a substance changes state. The particles are only rearranged.

cards.title: Diffusion and gas pressure
cards.question: What is diffusion, and what causes gas pressure?
points: Diffusion is particles spreading from where there are lots of them to where there are few.
It happens because particles move randomly. It is fastest in gases and does not happen in solids.
Diffusion is faster when it is warmer, because particles move faster.
Gas pressure is caused by gas particles hitting the walls of their container.
More particles or a higher temperature means more collisions, so higher pressure.
cards.watch_out: A balloon shrinks in the cold because the particles move slower and hit the walls less.

cards.title: Density
cards.question: How do you calculate density, and why are gases less dense than solids?
points: density = mass ÷ volume
Units: g/cm³ or kg/m³.
Solids are usually most dense and gases least dense, because gas particles are far apart.
An object floats in water if its density is less than water (1 g/cm³).

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A block has a mass of 200 g and a volume of 50 cm³.
density = 200 ÷ 50 = 4 g/cm³, so it sinks in water.

cards.watch_out: Ice is an exception. It is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats.

cards.title: Forces
cards.question: What is a force, and what is the difference between contact and non-contact forces?
points: A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N) with a newtonmeter.
Contact forces need objects to touch: friction, air resistance, water resistance, upthrust, tension, normal reaction (support).
Non-contact forces act at a distance: gravity, magnetic, electrostatic.
On a force diagram, the arrow length shows the size and the arrow points in the direction.
cards.watch_out: Weight is a force (in N). Mass is not a force (in kg).

cards.title: Resultant forces
cards.question: How do you work out a resultant force, and what happens when forces are balanced or unbalanced?
points: Same direction forces add. Opposite direction forces subtract.
Balanced forces (resultant zero): a still object stays still; a moving object keeps the same speed.
Unbalanced forces make an object speed up, slow down or change direction.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: 50 N to the right, 30 N to the left
resultant = 50 - 30 = 20 N to the right

cards.watch_out: Balanced forces do not mean the object is stopped. It could be moving at a steady speed.

cards.title: Friction, drag and stretching
cards.question: How do friction and drag affect motion, and how do springs stretch?
points: Friction acts against movement and heats up surfaces. Lubricants such as oil reduce it.
Drag (air or water resistance) gets bigger as speed increases. Streamlined shapes reduce it.
Forces can change an object's shape by stretching, squashing or bending.
Hooke's law: a spring's extension is proportional to the force, until the limit of proportionality.

example.heading: Spring example
lines: 1 N stretches a spring by 2 cm.
3 N stretches it by 6 cm (if under the limit).

cards.watch_out: Extension is how much longer the spring got, not its total length.

cards.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
cards.question: What is the difference between sexual and asexual reproduction?
points: Sexual reproduction: two parents. Sex cells (gametes) join at fertilisation.
Offspring of sexual reproduction are varied, not identical to their parents.
Asexual reproduction: one parent. Offspring are identical (clones).
Examples of asexual: bacteria splitting, strawberry runners, potato tubers.
cards.watch_out: Fertilisation is the joining of the nuclei of the two sex cells, not the act of mating.

cards.title: Reproductive organs and fertilisation
cards.question: What do the main male and female reproductive organs do, and where does fertilisation happen?
points: Testes make sperm and hormones. Sperm ducts carry sperm. Glands add fluid to make semen.
Ovaries release eggs. The oviduct (fallopian tube) carries the egg to the uterus.
The uterus (womb) is where a baby develops. The cervix is a ring of muscle at its opening.
Fertilisation happens in the oviduct when a sperm nucleus joins the egg nucleus.
cards.watch_out: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct, not in the uterus.

cards.title: Puberty
cards.question: What happens during puberty, and what causes the changes?
points: Puberty is when the body changes from a child to an adult. It is caused by sex hormones.
Hormones: testosterone in boys, oestrogen in girls.
Both: growth spurt, pubic and underarm hair, body odour.
Boys: voice breaks, testes start making sperm, facial hair, shoulders widen.
Girls: breasts develop, hips widen, periods start.
cards.watch_out: Puberty is the physical changes. Adolescence is the whole time of physical and emotional change.

cards.title: The menstrual cycle
cards.question: What happens during the 28-day menstrual cycle?
points: The cycle lasts about 28 days.
Days 1 to 5: period. The uterus lining breaks down and leaves the body.
The lining then builds up again, ready for a fertilised egg.
Around day 14: ovulation. An egg is released from an ovary.
If the egg is not fertilised, the lining breaks down and the cycle starts again.
cards.watch_out: Ovulation is the release of the egg, roughly halfway through the cycle.

cards.title: Embryo and fetus development
cards.question: How does a fertilised egg develop, and how does the placenta keep the fetus alive?
points: The fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells called an embryo, which implants in the uterus lining.
After about 8 weeks, once all organs have started to form, it is called a fetus.
The placenta lets oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother's blood, and waste such as carbon dioxide go back.
The umbilical cord joins the fetus to the placenta. Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus.
Pregnancy (gestation) lasts about 9 months.
cards.watch_out: The mother's and baby's blood do not mix. Substances diffuse across the placenta.

cards.title: Flowers and pollination
cards.question: What are the male and female parts of a flower, and how are flowers adapted for pollination?
points: Male part, the stamen: anther (makes pollen) on a filament.
Female part, the carpel: stigma (catches pollen), style, ovary (holds ovules).
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma.
Insect pollinated: bright petals, scent, nectar, sticky pollen.
Wind pollinated: small dull petals, anthers and stigmas hang outside, lots of light pollen.
cards.watch_out: Pollination is not fertilisation. Pollination moves pollen; fertilisation joins the nuclei.

cards.title: Fertilisation and seed dispersal in plants
cards.question: What happens after pollination, and how are seeds spread?
points: A pollen tube grows down the style into the ovary. The pollen nucleus joins the ovule nucleus.
The fertilised ovule becomes a seed. The ovary becomes a fruit.
Seeds are dispersed by wind (sycamore), animals (berries, burrs), water (coconut) or explosion (pea pods).
Dispersal stops new plants competing with the parent for light, water and minerals.
Germination needs water, oxygen and warmth.
cards.watch_out: Seeds do not need light to germinate. They need light once leaves grow.

cards.title: Atoms, elements and molecules
cards.question: What is the difference between an atom, an element and a molecule?
points: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
An element is made of only one type of atom. It cannot be split into simpler substances by chemistry.
Each element has a symbol of one or two letters, first letter a capital (O, Na, Fe).
A molecule is two or more atoms joined together, such as O₂ or H₂O.
cards.watch_out: Some symbols come from Latin names. Fe is iron, Na is sodium, Pb is lead.

cards.title: The periodic table
cards.question: How is the periodic table laid out, and what do groups and periods mean?
points: The periodic table lists all the elements.
Columns are groups. Elements in the same group have similar properties.
Rows are periods.
Metals are on the left and middle. Non-metals are on the right, past the staircase line.
Group 1: alkali metals (very reactive). Group 7: halogens. Group 0: noble gases (unreactive).
cards.watch_out: Groups go down. Periods go across.

cards.title: Metals and non-metals
cards.question: How are the properties of metals and non-metals different?
points: Metals: shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (can be hammered), ductile (can be pulled into wires), sonorous (ring), high melting points.
Non-metals: dull, poor conductors (insulators), brittle when solid, low melting points.
Many non-metals are gases at room temperature, such as oxygen and nitrogen.
Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. Graphite is a non-metal that conducts.
cards.watch_out: Most metals are not magnetic. The magnetic metals are iron, nickel and cobalt, and steel because it contains iron.

cards.title: Compounds and mixtures
cards.question: What is a compound, how do you name one, and how is it different from a mixture?
points: A compound is two or more elements chemically joined. Its properties differ from the elements.
Names ending in ide usually have two elements (sodium chloride); hydroxide is an exception. Names ending in ate also contain oxygen (copper sulfate).
Formulae show the atoms: H₂O is 2 hydrogen and 1 oxygen.
A mixture is substances that are not chemically joined. It can be separated by physical methods.

example.heading: Example
lines: sodium (reactive metal) + chlorine (toxic gas) → sodium chloride (table salt)

cards.watch_out: Air is a mixture. Water is a compound.

cards.title: Hazards in the lab
cards.question: What do the main hazard symbols mean, and how do you stay safe in practicals?
points: Flammable (flame): catches fire easily. Corrosive (hand and surface being eaten away): destroys skin.
Toxic (skull and crossbones): can cause death. Harmful or irritant (exclamation mark): can cause rashes or illness.
Oxidising (flame over a circle): helps other things burn.
Wear goggles, tie hair back, stand up in practicals, keep bags under desks.
Use the yellow safety flame on a Bunsen when not heating. The blue flame is hotter.
cards.watch_out: A hazard is something that could cause harm. A risk is how likely that harm is.

cards.title: Mass, weight and gravity
cards.question: What is the difference between mass and weight, and how do you calculate weight?
points: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms (kg). It is the same everywhere.
Weight is the force of gravity on a mass, in newtons (N). It changes on different planets.
weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g)
g on Earth is about 10 N/kg. g on the Moon is about 1.6 N/kg.
Gravity is stronger for bigger masses and when objects are closer.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A 50 kg student on Earth: 50 × 10 = 500 N
On the Moon: 50 × 1.6 = 80 N

cards.watch_out: An astronaut's mass does not change in space. Only their weight changes.

cards.title: The solar system
cards.question: What is in our solar system, and in what order are the planets?
points: The Sun is a star at the centre. Eight planets orbit it because of gravity.
Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. (My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming.)
The inner four are small and rocky. The outer four are giant planets made mostly of gas and ice. The asteroid belt is between Mars and Jupiter.
Planets further from the Sun take longer to orbit and are colder.
Our solar system is in the Milky Way galaxy. A light year is the distance light travels in one year.
cards.watch_out: A light year measures distance, not time.

cards.title: Days, years and seasons
cards.question: What causes day and night, a year, and the seasons?
points: Day and night: Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours.
A year: Earth orbits the Sun once every 365¼ days.
Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted.
UK summer: our half of Earth tilts towards the Sun, so days are longer and the Sun is higher in the sky.
The Moon orbits Earth about once a month. Its phases come from how much of its lit side we see.
cards.watch_out: Seasons are not caused by Earth being closer to the Sun. They are caused by the tilt.

cards.title: Ecosystems
cards.question: What do the words ecosystem, habitat, population and community mean?
points: Ecosystem: all the living things in an area plus their non-living surroundings.
Habitat: the place where an organism lives.
Population: the number of one species in an area.
Community: all the populations of different species in an area.
Interdependence means organisms depend on each other for food, shelter and pollination.
cards.watch_out: Population is one species. Community is many species.

cards.title: Food chains and food webs
cards.question: What do the arrows in a food chain show, and what happens in a food web when one population changes?
points: Arrows show the direction energy is transferred. They point from the food to the eater.
Producers (plants) make their own food by photosynthesis.
Then primary consumer (herbivore), secondary consumer, tertiary consumer. Top predator at the end.
A food web is lots of linked food chains.
If one population falls, its predators may fall and its prey may rise.

example.heading: Example chain
lines: grass → rabbit → fox
producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer

cards.watch_out: Toxic chemicals build up along a food chain (bioaccumulation), so top predators get the most.

cards.title: Sampling
cards.question: How do ecologists estimate the size of a population?
points: A quadrat is a square frame placed randomly to count plants or slow-moving animals.
Random placement avoids bias. More quadrats give a more reliable estimate.
Animals can be caught with pitfall traps, sweep nets, pooters and kick sampling in streams.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: Mean of 4 daisies per 1 m² quadrat. Field is 200 m².
Estimate = 4 × 200 = 800 daisies

cards.watch_out: Work out the mean per quadrat first, then multiply by the number of quadrats that fit in the area.

cards.title: Competition and adaptation
cards.question: What do plants and animals compete for, and how do adaptations help them survive?
points: Plants compete for light, water, minerals and space.
Animals compete for food, water, space (territory) and mates.
Organisms that are better adapted are more likely to survive and reproduce.
Polar bear: thick fur and fat for warmth, white fur for camouflage.
Cactus: spines instead of leaves to cut water loss, thick stem to store water.
cards.watch_out: Plants do not compete for food. They make their own food, so they compete for light.

cards.title: Pure substances and mixtures
cards.question: What does pure mean in science, and how can you tell a pure substance from a mixture?
points: A pure substance contains only one element or one compound.
A pure substance melts and boils at one exact temperature. Pure water boils at 100 °C.
A mixture melts or boils over a range of temperatures.
Air, sea water and ink are mixtures.
cards.watch_out: Pure orange juice on a carton is not pure in science. It is a mixture of many substances.

cards.title: Solutions and solubility
cards.question: What are a solute, solvent and solution, and what is a saturated solution?
points: A solute dissolves in a solvent to make a solution. Salt (solute) in water (solvent).
Soluble substances dissolve. Insoluble substances do not.
A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute.
Solubility usually increases as the temperature rises.

example.heading: Mass is conserved
lines: 100 g of water + 20 g of salt = 120 g of solution

cards.watch_out: Dissolving is not melting. Melting needs heat and only one substance.

cards.title: Filtration and evaporation
cards.question: How do you separate sand from water, and salt from salty water?
points: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, such as sand from water.
The solid left in the filter paper is the residue. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a solution, such as salt from salty water.
Heating gently or leaving the solution in a warm place gives larger crystals (crystallisation).

example.heading: Rock salt method
lines: 1. Crush rock salt and dissolve in warm water.
2. Filter to remove sand. 3. Evaporate the filtrate to get salt.

cards.watch_out: You cannot filter salt out of water. Dissolved particles are small enough to pass through.

cards.title: Distillation and chromatography
cards.question: How do distillation and chromatography separate mixtures?
points: Distillation gets the pure solvent from a solution, such as pure water from sea water.
The solution is boiled, the vapour is cooled in a condenser, and the pure liquid is collected.
Chromatography separates the dyes in an ink.
Draw the start line in pencil. Put the paper in solvent with the line above the solvent level.
The more soluble a dye, the further it travels up the paper.
cards.watch_out: Use pencil for the start line because pen ink would dissolve and run.

cards.title: Energy stores
cards.question: What are the energy stores, and what is the law of conservation of energy?
points: Kinetic (moving), gravitational potential (raised up), elastic (stretched or squashed), thermal (hot).
Chemical (food, fuel, batteries), nuclear, magnetic, electrostatic.
Energy is measured in joules (J). Food labels use kilojoules (kJ). 1 kJ = 1000 J.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another.
cards.watch_out: Light and sound are ways energy is transferred, not stores.

cards.title: Energy transfers and efficiency
cards.question: How is energy transferred, and how do you work out efficiency?
points: Energy is transferred by heating, by forces (mechanically), electrically, and by light and sound.
Useful energy goes where we want. Wasted energy usually spreads out as heat to the surroundings.
efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in (× 100 for a percentage)

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A bulb takes in 100 J and gives out 20 J of light.
efficiency = 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2 = 20%

cards.watch_out: No device is 100% efficient. Wasted energy is spread out, not destroyed.

cards.title: Temperature and conduction
cards.question: What is the difference between temperature and thermal energy, and how does conduction work?
points: Temperature tells you how hot something is, in °C. Thermal energy is measured in joules.
A bath of warm water can hold more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water, because it has more particles.
Energy flows from hotter objects to cooler ones until they reach the same temperature.
Conduction happens in solids. Particles vibrate and pass energy on to their neighbours.
Metals are good conductors. Insulators include plastic, wood and air.
cards.watch_out: Cold does not flow in. Heat flows out from the warmer object.

cards.title: Convection, radiation and insulation
cards.question: How do convection and radiation transfer energy, and how can a house lose less heat?
points: Convection happens in liquids and gases. Warm fluid is less dense, so it rises; cool fluid sinks.
This makes a convection current, such as the warm air above a radiator.
Radiation is infrared waves. It needs no particles, so it can travel through space.
Dark matt surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers. Shiny surfaces reflect radiation.
Insulation traps air: loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, double glazing.
cards.watch_out: Convection cannot happen in a solid because the particles cannot move around.

cards.title: Series and parallel circuits
cards.question: What is the difference between a series circuit and a parallel circuit?
points: Current only flows if the circuit is a complete loop.
Series: one loop. If one bulb breaks, they all go out. More bulbs make each one dimmer.
Parallel: more than one branch. If one bulb breaks, the others stay on. Each bulb stays bright.
Homes are wired in parallel so each appliance can be switched on and off on its own.
Symbols to know: cell, battery, bulb, open and closed switch, ammeter (A in a circle), voltmeter (V in a circle), resistor, motor, buzzer.
cards.watch_out: A battery is two or more cells joined together.

cards.title: Current
cards.question: What is current, how is it measured, and how does it behave in series and parallel?
points: Current is the flow of charge around a circuit. It is measured in amps (A).
Measure current with an ammeter placed in series.
Series: the current is the same everywhere in the loop.
Parallel: the current splits at a junction. The branch currents add up to the total.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: Total current 0.6 A. One branch has 0.2 A.
Other branch = 0.6 - 0.2 = 0.4 A

cards.watch_out: Current is not used up by bulbs. The same current that leaves the cell comes back to it.

cards.title: Voltage and resistance
cards.question: What are voltage and resistance, and how do you calculate resistance?
points: Voltage (potential difference) is the push from the cell. It is measured in volts (V).
Measure voltage with a voltmeter placed in parallel across a component.
Series: voltages across the components add up to the cell voltage. Parallel: each branch gets the full voltage.
Resistance is how hard it is for current to flow, in ohms (Ω). resistance = voltage ÷ current

example.heading: Worked example
lines: 6 V across a bulb, 2 A through it
resistance = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 Ω

cards.watch_out: Ammeter goes in series. Voltmeter goes in parallel. Higher resistance means lower current.

cards.title: Equations to learn
cards.question: Can you write each equation and its units from memory?
points: speed (m/s) = distance (m) ÷ time (s)
pressure (N/m²) = force (N) ÷ area (m²)
density (g/cm³) = mass (g) ÷ volume (cm³)
weight (N) = mass (kg) × g (N/kg)
resistance (Ω) = voltage (V) ÷ current (A)
magnification = eyepiece × objective. efficiency = useful out ÷ total in
cards.watch_out: Write the equation, put the numbers in, then give the answer with a unit. Each step can earn a mark.

cards.title: Word equations to learn
cards.question: Can you complete each general word equation and gas test?
points: acid + alkali → salt + water
acid + metal → salt + hydrogen (squeaky pop)
acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (limewater milky)
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (photosynthesis)
hydrochloric → chloride, sulfuric → sulfate, nitric → nitrate
cards.watch_out: Count the products. Carbonate reactions make three products; metal reactions make two.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT a job of the skeleton?
mcq.e: The skeleton supports, protects, helps movement and makes blood cells. Digestion is done by the digestive system.

mcq.q: Which part of the skeleton protects the brain?
mcq.e: The skull surrounds the brain.

mcq.q: Where are new blood cells made?
mcq.e: Bone marrow in the centre of some bones makes blood cells.

mcq.q: What type of joint is the knee?
mcq.e: The knee bends in one direction like a door hinge.

mcq.q: What type of joint is the hip?
mcq.e: The hip can move in many directions.

mcq.q: What joins a muscle to a bone?
mcq.e: Tendons join muscle to bone. Ligaments join bone to bone.

mcq.q: What joins one bone to another bone at a joint?
mcq.e: Ligaments hold bones together at joints.

mcq.q: What does cartilage do at a joint?
mcq.a: Stops the ends of bones rubbing together
mcq.e: Cartilage is a smooth cushion on the ends of bones.

mcq.q: When you bend your arm what do the biceps and triceps do?
mcq.e: The biceps pulls the forearm up while the triceps relaxes.

mcq.q: Why do muscles work in antagonistic pairs?
mcq.a: Muscles can only pull and not push
mcq.e: Each muscle can only contract and pull, so a second muscle is needed to move the bone back.

mcq.q: What is the correct order for air entering the lungs?
mcq.a: Trachea then bronchi then bronchioles then alveoli
w: Bronchi then trachea then alveoli then bronchioles
Alveoli then bronchioles then bronchi then trachea
Trachea then alveoli then bronchi then bronchioles
mcq.e: Air passes down the trachea into ever smaller tubes and ends in the alveoli.

mcq.q: Where does gas exchange take place?
mcq.e: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the alveoli walls.

mcq.q: Which is NOT an adaptation of the alveoli?
mcq.e: Alveoli walls are only one cell thick so gases diffuse quickly.

mcq.q: What happens to the diaphragm when you breathe in?
mcq.e: A flattening diaphragm makes the chest bigger.

mcq.q: When you breathe in what happens to the volume and pressure in your chest?
mcq.e: Bigger volume means lower pressure so air flows in.

mcq.q: In the bell jar model what do the balloons represent?
mcq.e: The balloons inflate like the lungs. The rubber sheet is the diaphragm.

mcq.q: Compared with breathed in air breathed out air contains
mcq.a: More carbon dioxide and less oxygen
w: More oxygen and less carbon dioxide
The same amount of both gases
mcq.e: Cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide in respiration.

mcq.q: What is a drug?
mcq.a: A chemical that changes the way the body works
mcq.e: Drugs can be medicinal or recreational.

mcq.q: Which of these is a medicinal drug?
mcq.e: Paracetamol is a painkiller taken for health.

mcq.q: Alcohol is a depressant. What does this mean?
mcq.a: It slows down the nervous system
w: It makes you feel sad only
mcq.e: Depressants slow down nerve signals so reactions are slower.

mcq.q: Which substance in cigarette smoke causes cancer?
mcq.e: Tar contains chemicals that cause cancer.

mcq.q: Which substance in cigarette smoke is addictive?
mcq.e: Nicotine causes addiction.

mcq.q: What does xylem carry?
mcq.e: Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem carries sugars.

mcq.q: Why do root hair cells have long thin extensions?
mcq.a: To give a large surface area to absorb water
mcq.e: More surface area means more water and minerals are absorbed.

mcq.q: What do stomata in a leaf do?
mcq.a: Let gases in and out of the leaf
mcq.e: Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen and water vapour leave through stomata.

mcq.q: Which layer of a leaf has the most chloroplasts?
mcq.e: Palisade cells are near the top where light is strongest.

mcq.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
mcq.e: pH 7 is neutral. Below is acid, above is alkali.

mcq.q: Which pH is the strongest acid?
mcq.e: The lower the pH the more acidic.

mcq.q: A solution has a pH of 12. It is
mcq.e: pH 12 is high on the scale so it is strongly alkaline.

mcq.q: Which of these is an acid?
mcq.e: Vinegar contains ethanoic acid.

mcq.q: Which of these is an alkali?
mcq.e: Sodium hydroxide is a common lab alkali.

mcq.q: What is an alkali?
mcq.a: A base that dissolves in water
w: A salt that does not dissolve
mcq.e: All alkalis are bases but not all bases dissolve.

mcq.q: What colour does litmus turn in acid?
mcq.e: Litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali.

mcq.q: What colour is universal indicator in a neutral solution?
mcq.e: Green shows pH 7.

mcq.q: Universal indicator turns purple. The solution is
mcq.e: Purple is at the high end of the pH scale.

mcq.q: Why is universal indicator more useful than litmus?
mcq.a: It shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is
mcq.e: Universal indicator has a range of colours for different pH values.

mcq.q: What are the products when an acid reacts with an alkali?
mcq.e: acid + alkali gives salt + water. This is neutralisation.

mcq.q: What happens to the pH when alkali is slowly added to an acid?
mcq.e: The alkali neutralises the acid so the pH goes up.

mcq.q: Why do people take indigestion tablets?
w: To make the stomach more acidic
To add more acid to food
mcq.e: Indigestion tablets contain a base.

mcq.q: Which salt is made from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide?
mcq.e: Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides.

mcq.q: Which acid makes sulfate salts?
mcq.e: Sulfuric acid makes sulfates.

mcq.q: Which acid makes nitrate salts?
mcq.e: Nitric acid makes nitrates.

mcq.q: What gas is made when a metal reacts with an acid?
mcq.e: metal + acid gives salt + hydrogen.

mcq.q: What is the test for hydrogen?
mcq.a: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
mcq.e: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.

mcq.q: What are the products when calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid?
mcq.e: Carbonates make a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

mcq.q: What is the test for carbon dioxide?
mcq.e: Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy.

mcq.q: Complete the equation. magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + ...
mcq.e: A metal and an acid make a salt and hydrogen.

mcq.q: Which hazard symbol would be on a bottle of concentrated acid?
mcq.e: Concentrated acids destroy skin and surfaces.

mcq.q: What is the equation for speed?
mcq.e: Speed is distance travelled each second.

mcq.q: A car travels 300 m in 15 s. What is its speed?
A cyclist travels at 5 m/s for 60 s. How far do they go?
mcq.e: distance = speed × time = 5 × 60.

mcq.q: A train travels 120 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
Which unit is used for speed?
mcq.e: Speed is metres per second.

mcq.q: Two cars drive the same way at 30 m/s and 25 m/s. What is their relative speed?
mcq.e: Same direction so subtract. 30 - 25 = 5 m/s.

mcq.q: On a distance-time graph what does a horizontal line show?
w: The object has a steady high speed
mcq.e: Distance is not changing so it has stopped.

mcq.q: On a distance-time graph a steeper line means
mcq.e: More distance in the same time means faster.

mcq.q: A straight sloping line on a distance-time graph shows
mcq.e: A constant slope means the same distance every second.

mcq.q: A curved line getting steeper on a distance-time graph shows
mcq.e: The slope is increasing so the speed is increasing.

mcq.q: A graph line rises 80 m in 10 s. What is the speed?
What is the equation for pressure?
mcq.e: Pressure is force spread over an area.

mcq.q: A force of 200 N acts on an area of 4 m². What is the pressure?
A box of weight 60 N sits on an area of 20 cm². What is the pressure?
Why do snowshoes stop you sinking into snow?
mcq.a: They spread your weight over a larger area so the pressure is lower
mcq.e: Bigger area means less pressure.

mcq.q: Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt one?
mcq.a: The small area gives a high pressure
w: The small area gives a low pressure
mcq.e: Same force on a smaller area gives higher pressure.

mcq.q: Which unit is a unit of pressure?
mcq.e: Pressure is newtons per square metre (pascals).

mcq.q: Why are dams thicker at the bottom?
w: Water is lighter at the bottom
mcq.e: The deeper water pushes harder on the dam.

mcq.q: Holes are made at the top middle and bottom of a bottle of water. Which hole does the water spurt furthest from?
mcq.e: Pressure is highest at the bottom.

mcq.q: Why does atmospheric pressure fall as you climb a mountain?
mcq.a: There is less air above you pushing down
w: There is more air above you
mcq.e: Fewer air particles above means lower pressure.

mcq.q: What causes the pressure of a gas in a container?
mcq.a: Particles hitting the walls of the container
mcq.e: Each collision pushes on the wall.

mcq.q: A boat floats on water. Which is true?
mcq.a: Upthrust equals the weight of the boat
mcq.e: Balanced forces mean the boat floats.

mcq.q: Which part of a cell controls its activities?
mcq.e: The nucleus holds genetic material and controls the cell.

mcq.q: Where does respiration happen in a cell?
mcq.e: Mitochondria release energy by respiration.

mcq.q: Which part is found in plant cells but NOT animal cells?
mcq.e: Plant cells also have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole.

mcq.q: What do chloroplasts do?
mcq.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll which absorbs light.

mcq.q: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
mcq.a: To leave more room to carry oxygen
mcq.e: No nucleus means more space for oxygen carrying haemoglobin.

mcq.q: A microscope has a x10 eyepiece and a x40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
Which objective lens should you start with?
mcq.e: Low power makes it easier to find the sample first.

mcq.q: What is the correct order of organisation from smallest to largest?
mcq.a: Cell then tissue then organ then organ system
w: Organ then tissue then cell then organ system
Tissue then cell then organ then organ system
Cell then organ then tissue then organ system
mcq.e: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems.

mcq.q: In which state are particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions?
mcq.e: Gas particles have large gaps and move fast.

mcq.q: How do particles move in a solid?
w: They move freely in all directions
They do not move at all
mcq.e: Solid particles are held in place but vibrate.

mcq.q: What is the change of state from gas to liquid called?
mcq.e: Condensation turns a gas into a liquid.

mcq.q: What is sublimation?
mcq.a: A solid turning straight into a gas
w: A liquid turning into a solid
A gas turning into a liquid
mcq.e: Dry ice sublimes.

mcq.q: Why does diffusion happen faster when it is warmer?
mcq.e: More energy means faster particles.

mcq.q: A block has a mass of 120 g and a volume of 40 cm³. What is its density?
Why can gases be compressed but solids cannot?
mcq.a: Gas particles have large gaps between them
mcq.e: The gaps let gas particles be pushed closer.

mcq.q: What is force measured in?
mcq.e: Force is measured in newtons (N).

mcq.q: Which is a non-contact force?
mcq.e: Gravity acts without touching.

mcq.q: Forces of 40 N right and 15 N left act on a box. What is the resultant force?
mcq.e: Opposite directions so subtract. 40 - 15 = 25 N right.

mcq.q: The forces on a moving car are balanced. What happens?
mcq.a: It keeps moving at the same speed
mcq.e: Balanced forces mean no change in motion.

mcq.q: Which reduces friction?
mcq.e: Lubricants let surfaces slide easily.

mcq.q: What happens to air resistance as a cyclist goes faster?
mcq.e: Drag increases with speed.

mcq.q: A 2 N force stretches a spring 4 cm. What will 4 N stretch it by (below the limit)?
mcq.e: Doubling the force doubles the extension.

mcq.q: How many parents are needed for asexual reproduction?
mcq.e: Asexual offspring are clones of one parent.

mcq.q: Where does fertilisation happen in humans?
mcq.e: The sperm meets the egg in the oviduct.

mcq.q: What do the testes make?
mcq.e: The testes make sperm and testosterone.

mcq.q: Which hormone causes puberty in girls?
mcq.e: Oestrogen controls female changes at puberty.

mcq.q: Around which day of the menstrual cycle does ovulation happen?
mcq.e: An egg is released about halfway through the cycle.

mcq.q: What is the job of the placenta?
mcq.a: Exchanging oxygen nutrients and waste between mother and fetus
w: Protecting the fetus from all bumps
mcq.e: Substances diffuse across the placenta.

mcq.q: What is pollination?
mcq.a: Transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
w: Joining of pollen and ovule nuclei
Growing a new plant from a seed
mcq.e: Pollination comes before fertilisation.

mcq.q: Which feature suggests a flower is wind pollinated?
mcq.a: Anthers that hang outside the flower
mcq.e: Wind pollinated flowers expose anthers and stigmas to the wind.

mcq.q: After fertilisation in a plant the ovary becomes the
mcq.e: The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

mcq.q: What is an element?
mcq.a: A substance made of only one type of atom
mcq.e: Elements cannot be broken down chemically.

mcq.q: What is the symbol for iron?
mcq.e: Fe comes from the Latin word ferrum.

mcq.q: In the periodic table what is a column called?
mcq.e: Elements in a group have similar properties.

mcq.q: Which is a property of most metals?
mcq.e: Metals conduct heat and electricity well.

mcq.q: Which metal is magnetic?
mcq.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are the magnetic metals.

mcq.q: Which is a compound?
mcq.e: Water is hydrogen and oxygen chemically joined.

mcq.q: Which hazard symbol means a substance catches fire easily?
mcq.e: The flammable symbol is a flame.

mcq.q: What is weight measured in?
mcq.e: Weight is a force so it is in newtons.

mcq.q: A 40 kg child is on Earth where g = 10 N/kg. What is their weight?
An astronaut goes from Earth to the Moon. What happens?
mcq.a: Mass stays the same and weight decreases
w: Mass decreases and weight stays the same
mcq.e: The Moon has weaker gravity but mass is unchanged.

mcq.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
mcq.e: Mercury is the first planet.

mcq.q: What is a light year?
mcq.a: The distance light travels in one year
w: The time it takes light to reach Earth
mcq.e: A light year is a distance.

mcq.q: What causes day and night?
mcq.a: The Earth spinning on its axis
mcq.e: One spin takes 24 hours.

mcq.q: What causes the seasons?
mcq.a: The tilt of the Earth's axis
w: The Earth's distance from the Sun
The Sun getting hotter in summer
mcq.e: The tilt changes day length and how high the Sun is.

mcq.q: What is a habitat?
mcq.a: The place where an organism lives
w: All the organisms in an area
mcq.e: A habitat is an organism's home.

mcq.q: What is a population?
mcq.a: The number of one species in an area
w: All the species in an area
mcq.e: Population is one species only.

mcq.q: In a food chain what do the arrows show?
mcq.e: Arrows point from food to eater.

mcq.q: What is a producer?
mcq.a: An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis
mcq.e: Plants are producers.

mcq.q: In grass → rabbit → fox the rabbit is the
mcq.e: The rabbit is the first animal in the chain.

mcq.q: A mean of 3 buttercups is found per 1 m² quadrat in a 50 m² field. Estimate the population.
mcq.e: 3 × 50 = 150 buttercups.

mcq.q: What do plants compete for?
mcq.e: Plants make their own food so they compete for what they need to make it.

mcq.q: In salty water what is the solvent?
mcq.e: The solvent is the liquid the solute dissolves in.

mcq.q: What is a saturated solution?
mcq.a: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute
mcq.e: Extra solute stays undissolved.

mcq.q: 50 g of sugar dissolves in 200 g of water. What is the mass of the solution?
mcq.e: Mass is conserved. 200 + 50 = 250 g.

mcq.q: Which method separates sand from water?
mcq.e: Sand is insoluble so it is caught in the filter paper.

mcq.q: Which method gets pure water from sea water?
mcq.e: The water is boiled and the vapour is condensed.

mcq.q: Which method separates the dyes in an ink?
mcq.e: Different dyes travel different distances up the paper.

mcq.q: How can you tell that a substance is pure?
mcq.a: It melts at one exact temperature
w: It melts over a range of temperatures
It says pure on the label
mcq.e: Mixtures melt over a range.

mcq.q: What is energy measured in?
mcq.e: Energy is measured in joules (J).

mcq.q: Which energy store does a stretched elastic band have?
mcq.e: Stretched or squashed objects store elastic energy.

mcq.q: Which energy store does food have?
mcq.e: Food fuel and batteries are chemical stores.

mcq.q: What does the law of conservation of energy say?
mcq.a: Energy cannot be created or destroyed
w: Energy can be made from nothing
Energy is only stored as heat
mcq.e: Energy is only transferred between stores.

mcq.q: A kettle takes in 2000 J and 1600 J heats the water. What is its efficiency?
How is energy transferred through a metal spoon?
mcq.e: Vibrating particles pass energy along the solid.

mcq.q: Why does loft insulation reduce heat loss?
mcq.a: It traps air which is a poor conductor
w: It makes the loft hotter by itself
It adds more particles that conduct well
mcq.e: Trapped air reduces conduction and convection.

mcq.q: What is current measured in?
mcq.e: Current is measured in amps (A).

mcq.q: How should an ammeter be connected?
mcq.e: An ammeter goes in the loop so current flows through it.

mcq.q: How should a voltmeter be connected?
mcq.e: A voltmeter compares the push either side of a component.

mcq.q: In a series circuit one bulb breaks. What happens?
mcq.e: The single loop is broken.

mcq.q: A current of 0.9 A splits into two branches. One branch has 0.3 A. What is in the other?
mcq.e: Branch currents add up to the total. 0.9 - 0.3 = 0.6 A.

mcq.q: A bulb has 12 V across it and 3 A through it. What is its resistance?
mcq.e: resistance = voltage ÷ current = 12 ÷ 3.

mcq.q: Why are homes wired in parallel?
mcq.a: Each appliance can be switched on and off on its own
w: It uses less wire than anything else
mcq.e: Each branch is its own loop.

written.q: Describe how the diaphragm and ribs move to make air enter the lungs. Explain why air moves in.
model: Diaphragm contracts and flattens (1)
Intercostal muscles contract and ribs move up and out (1)
Volume of the chest increases so pressure inside falls (1)
Air moves from higher pressure outside to lower pressure inside (1)

written.q: Explain how the biceps and triceps work together to straighten the arm.
model: Muscles can only pull or contract (1)
Triceps contracts (1)
Biceps relaxes at the same time so they are an antagonistic pair (1)

written.q: Give three ways the alveoli are adapted for gas exchange.
model: Walls one cell thick so short distance for diffusion (1)
Large surface area (1)
Good blood supply or moist lining (1)

written.q: A student adds sodium hydroxide to hydrochloric acid with universal indicator. Describe the colour change and name the products.
model: Starts red or orange because acid (1)
Turns green at neutral pH 7 (1)
Products are sodium chloride and water (1)

written.q: Zinc reacts with sulfuric acid. Write the word equation and describe a test for the gas made.
model: zinc + sulfuric acid (1)
→ zinc sulfate + hydrogen (1)
Hold a lit splint at the mouth of the tube (1)
Squeaky pop shows hydrogen (1)

written.q: Explain why farmers might add lime to a field.
model: Soil is too acidic for crops (1)
Lime is a base that neutralises the acid and raises the pH (1)

written.q: A bus travels 1.2 km in 4 minutes. Calculate its speed in m/s.
model: speed = distance ÷ time = 1200 ÷ 240 (1)

written.q: Explain why a tractor has wide tyres to drive across a muddy field.
model: Wide tyres have a large area (1)
Pressure = force ÷ area so the pressure is smaller (1)
Tractor is less likely to sink into the mud (1)

written.q: Describe the journey shown by a distance-time graph that has a steep straight line then a flat line then a gentler straight line.
model: Steep line is a fast steady speed (1)
Flat line means stopped or stationary (1)
Gentle line is a slower steady speed (1)

written.q: Describe how to get pure dry salt from a mixture of sand and salt.
model: Add water and stir so the salt dissolves (1)
Filter to remove the sand as residue (1)
Heat the filtrate to evaporate the water (1)
Salt crystals are left (1)

written.q: A motor takes in 500 J of energy and transfers 350 J usefully. Calculate its efficiency.
model: efficiency = 350 ÷ 500 (1)

written.q: Name three parts found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell and give the job of each.
model: Cell wall strengthens the cell (1)
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis (1)
Permanent vacuole holds cell sap and keeps the cell firm (1)

section_a: Read the question twice. Underline NOT, BEST and MOST.
Cover the options and answer in your head first, then find your answer.
Cross out options you know are wrong. If two are left, pick the one that matches a key word from your flashcards.
Never leave one blank. A guess has a 1 in 4 chance.
For calculations, do the sum on paper. Wrong options are often the numbers multiplied instead of divided.
section_b: Count the marks. 3 marks means three separate points.
Describe means say what happens. Explain means say what happens AND why (use because or so).
Use the key words, such as diffuses, contracts, neutralises, pressure, area.
Calculations: equation, numbers in, answer, unit.
Check units match before you calculate (km to m, minutes to seconds, cm² or m²).
exam_tips.timing: About 35 minutes for the 45 multiple choice questions (under a minute each), then 15 minutes for the written answers.

vocab.meaning: To look at something in detail to understand it
vocab.example: Scientists analyse their results to find a pattern.

vocab.meaning: To judge how good or useful something is
vocab.example: Evaluate the bell jar model by giving a strength and a weakness.

vocab.meaning: To say what you think will happen
vocab.example: Predict what will happen to the pH when alkali is added.

vocab.meaning: Close to the true value
vocab.example: An accurate thermometer shows the true temperature.

vocab.meaning: Very exact, with repeat results close together
vocab.example: A precise balance measures to 0.01 g.

vocab.meaning: An idea that can be tested
vocab.example: My hypothesis is that longer springs stretch more.

vocab.meaning: What you decide after looking at the evidence
vocab.example: My conclusion is that speed increases with slope.

vocab.meaning: Facts or results that show something is true
vocab.example: Limewater turning milky is evidence of carbon dioxide.

vocab.meaning: Something that can change in an experiment
vocab.example: Temperature is the variable I changed.

vocab.meaning: Something that happens because of something else
vocab.example: One consequence of smoking is damaged cilia.

vocab.meaning: Large or important enough to notice
vocab.example: There was a significant increase in pressure.

vocab.meaning: Enough for what is needed
vocab.example: Plants need sufficient light to photosynthesise.

vocab.meaning: Present in large amounts
vocab.example: Oxygen is abundant in the air we breathe.

vocab.meaning: To move from one place to another
vocab.example: Energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat.

vocab.meaning: To take in
vocab.example: Root hair cells absorb water from the soil.

vocab.meaning: To let something go or give it out
vocab.example: Respiration releases energy from glucose.

vocab.meaning: To spread out evenly in a liquid so you cannot see it
vocab.example: Sugar dissolves in water to make a solution.

vocab.meaning: Working well without wasting energy
vocab.example: An LED is more efficient than an old bulb.

vocab.meaning: To let heat or electricity pass through
vocab.example: Metals conduct electricity well.

vocab.meaning: To become bigger or more
vocab.example: Pressure increases with depth.

vocab.meaning: To become smaller or less
vocab.example: Atmospheric pressure decreases as you climb.

vocab.meaning: To become shorter or tighter
vocab.example: The biceps contracts to bend the arm.

vocab.meaning: To become less tight
vocab.example: The triceps relaxes when the biceps contracts.

vocab.meaning: Neither acid nor alkali, pH 7
vocab.example: Pure water is neutral.

vocab.meaning: Able to destroy skin and materials
vocab.example: Concentrated acid is corrosive.

vocab.meaning: Not moving
vocab.example: A flat line on a distance-time graph means stationary.

vocab.meaning: Produced as a result, the overall effect
vocab.example: The resultant force is 20 N to the right.

vocab.meaning: A feature that helps a living thing survive
vocab.example: Thick fur is an adaptation for the cold.

vocab.meaning: Relying on each other
vocab.example: Bees and flowers are interdependent.

vocab.meaning: To spread out from where there is a lot to where there is little
vocab.example: Perfume diffuses across a room.
